title: How Sneezing Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how sneezing works, starting with the nasal filtration system, cilia, mast cells and histamine, and the afferent and efferent phases of the sneeze reflex. They cover the sneezing center in the lateral medulla (including a fisherman case that helped locate it), the muscles and speed involved, and common triggers across the types of rhinitis. Other topics include photic sneezing and its genetics, rare sneeze triggers such as eating too much, sexual arousal and orgasm, intractable sneezing (Donna Griffiths record), sneezing and contagion from the MIT droplet study, cultural "bless you" customs and superstitions, and myths about eyes popping out or the heart stopping. The episode closes with listener mail about Atlanta, Texas.
topics: autosomal dominant compelling helio-ophthalmic outburst syndrome

segments.title: Cold open
segments.summary: Josh introduces the spring allergy season and the episode on sneezing.

segments.title: Opening banter and word origin
segments.summary: Hosts banter about the show's opening and the word sternutation, which dates to a 1576 text.

segments.title: Sneezing as a bodily defense
segments.summary: Sneezing is described as an ancient reflex shared by mammals, with iguanas noted for sneezing often. Chuck explains it as the body's bouncer expelling irritants.

segments.title: Nasal filtration and irritant detection
segments.summary: Narrow nasal passages create turbulence that pushes air to the mucosa, where cilia move particles back to the throat. Particles that stick irritate mast cells, which release histamine and send signals to the brain.

segments.title: Afferent and efferent phases and nerve pathways
segments.summary: The sneeze takes under a second. The afferent phase is the irritation signal traveling through the olfactory, ethmoidal and trigeminal nerves to the sneeze center; the efferent phase is the response sent back.

segments.title: Muscles, pressure and speed of a sneeze
segments.summary: The sneeze involves many muscles, vocal cords clamping and then opening, and a diaphragm push at about one hundred miles per hour. The myth that eyes pop out when sneezing with eyes open is debunked.

segments.title: Involuntary nature of sneezing
segments.summary: Sneezing is involuntary and cannot be reliably triggered on command, though some things can trigger it.

segments.title: Sneezing center in the lateral medulla
segments.summary: The sneezing center was hypothesized from cat research and confirmed in humans around 2005 through a fisherman case with a lesion on the lateral medulla. Capsaicin tests showed he would not sneeze though his nose burned.

segments.title: Causes of rhinitis
segments.summary: Rhinitis, inflammation of the nasal mucous membrane, is the most common cause of sneezing. Types discussed include occupational, hormonal, drug-induced, and atrophic rhinitis, plus rhinorrhea for a runny nose.

segments.title: Chuck and Josh on sneezing commentary
segments.summary: Brief tangents on the rhinitis discussion and a remark about 2020.

segments.title: Photic sneezing and its genetics
segments.summary: Josh is a photic sneezer triggered by bright sunlight. Chuck and Josh discuss multiple sneezes in a row and the inherited photic sneeze reflex, with a crossover between the pupillary light reflex and sneeze reflex arcs. Looking toward the sun can help complete a stuck sneeze.

segments.title: Gustatory sneezing and evolutionary theory
segments.summary: Gustatory sneezing after eating is mentioned as rare. A theory connects photic sneezing to infants who cannot blow their noses.

segments.title: Unusual sneeze triggers
segments.summary: Plucking nose or eyebrow hairs can trigger sneezing or watering eyes via the trigeminal nerve. Sneezing from sexual arousal or orgasm is discussed, with an informal internet survey and a journal explanation involving erectile tissue in the nose.

segments.title: Intractable sneezing and Donna Griffiths
segments.summary: Intractable (psychogenic) sneezing mostly affects adolescent girls. Donna Griffiths sneezed for 977 days from January 1981 to September 1983. Sneezing during sleep is not possible, so she averaged about a sneeze a minute while awake.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Ad break between segments.

segments.title: Sneeze droplets and airborne spread
segments.summary: A 2016 MIT study by Lydia Bourouiba used high-speed film to show sneeze clouds of fluid that break into smaller particles, which can travel up to about 25 to 27 feet and remain suspended. Covering the nose and mouth and using masks are recommended. Chuck cites covering a sneeze with the elbow.

segments.title: Outdoor versus indoor spread during the pandemic
segments.summary: Josh summarizes an aerosol study on outdoor spread, noting outdoor air disperses particles more than indoor air. The hosts share personal experiences of avoiding people who sneeze during the pandemic.

segments.title: Bless you customs and sneeze folklore
segments.summary: Gregory I is said to have urged saying God bless you during the plague, while earlier Christians ignored sneezes according to Wilson D. Wallace's 1919 article. Greek and Roman phrases, a micro-affection concept, and a Zoroastrian belief about expelling a fiend are discussed.

segments.title: Sneeze omens and the heart-stopping myth
segments.summary: Sneezes are read as omens in China and Japan. The myth that the heart stops during a sneeze is debunked; heart electrical activity stays the same.

segments.title: Sneezing and pregnancy myth and throat rupture
segments.summary: A myth about sneezing after sex preventing pregnancy is mentioned. A man in Leicester was reported to have ruptured his throat trying to stifle a sneeze.

segments.title: Listener mail: Atlanta, Texas
segments.summary: Listener Benjamin Boden Lee writes about Atlanta, Texas, the town named in the Radio Atlanta pirate radio episode, and nearby Texarkana and the film Smokey and the Bandit.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and give the contact address and credits.
